chapterTitle: Understanding Unity's Input Systems: Old vs. New
aiGenerationNote: Create a 12-minute mixed-media lesson. Start with a slide deck comparing the legacy `Input` class (showing `Input.GetAxis` code) with the new Input System's benefits (flexibility, remapping). Transition to a live Unity Editor demo: install the Input System Package, create a `PlayerControls` Input Action Asset, define `Gameplay` Action Map, `Move` (Vector2) and `Jump` (Button) actions, and add keyboard (WASD/Space) and gamepad (left stick/A button) bindings. Highlight the "Save Asset" button. Include a side-by-side view of the Input Action Asset editor and the Project window. End with a 2-question interactive quiz about choosing the right input system for a given scenario. Focus on a professional, hands-on, and safety-conscious tone, emphasizing the importance of robust input for gameplay.

screens.title: Understanding Unity's Input Systems: Old vs. New
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll build a practical understanding of how Unity handles player input, and why the modern Input System Package is a different way of thinking. Historically, Unity exposed input through the Input class and a set of named axes and buttons. That worked for simple cases but became hard to scale as control schemes grew. The new Input System flips the approach: you define actions like Jump or Move, then map multiple physical controls to those actions. You’ll learn when to keep the legacy manager, when to adopt the package, and how to set up an Input Action Asset that makes runtime remapping and multiple control schemes manageable. We’ll also cover action maps, bindings, processors and interactions so you can make inputs feel responsive. By the end you will be able to configure a PlayerControls asset that supports keyboard and gamepad movement, and you’ll know the common migration mistakes to avoid. Think about your last game prototype: could abstracting inputs into actions simplify your code and make controls more robust for players?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Understanding Unity's Input Systems
Understanding Unity's Input Systems: Old vs. New
Learn why action-based input simplifies remapping, multi-device support, and context switches in modern games.
In this lesson
Compare the legacy Input Manager and the Input System Package, create an Input Action Asset for movement and jump, and learn common migration pitfalls.
Why it matters
Better input management reduces fragile conditional code, improves device support, and lets players remap controls cleanly at runtime.
Explore Key Topics
Legacy Input Manager
Axis names and Input.GetAxis calls configured in Project Settings.
Input System Package
Action-based approach, action maps, and broad device support.
Input Action Asset
Central asset defining actions, bindings, processors, and interactions.

Action
Jump

Binding

WASD, Arrow keys, Left stick
These cards represent the conceptual link: actions are device-agnostic commands, bindings connect physical controls, and processors or interactions tune responsiveness.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your work with Unity’s input systems so you learn both theory and practice. First, you will be able to differentiate between the legacy Input Manager and the Input System Package: know the role of Input. GetAxis and configured axes versus action-based mappings. Second, you will understand why the Input System Package is advantageous for flexibility, remapping, and multi-device support by exploring action maps, bindings, and event-driven callbacks. Third, you will configure the Input System Package in a project and create an Input Action Asset that defines action maps like Gameplay and UI plus actions like Move and Jump. Fourth, you will identify common pitfalls when migrating—such as disabling legacy input unexpectedly or misusing processors—and plan remedies. Each objective pairs a concrete task with a reason why it matters so you can both perform the steps and evaluate when to adopt the new system in real projects.

screens.title: The Legacy Input Manager: How it works
screens.narratorSegment: The legacy Input Manager is Unity’s original way of getting player input. It centers on the Input class and a set of named axes and buttons configured in Project Settings. In practice you call functions like Input. GetAxis with a logical axis name such as Horizontal, and Unity returns a float based on keyboard or joystick input mapped to that axis. This approach made small projects easy because you could centralize mappings and poll in Update. A concrete example is movement: many projects use an axis named Horizontal that maps the A and D keys, left and right arrow keys, and the joystick X-axis. That single axis return value drives character motion. A common misconception is that this system automatically supports many devices: it does work for keyboards and basic gamepads but struggles with diverse devices, fine-grained remapping, or separate control contexts. The main takeaway is that the legacy manager works well when control requirements are simple and fixed, but it becomes brittle as you add remapping, multiple players, or XR controllers. Keep this definition in mind when we compare it to the action-based model that follows.

screens.title: Where the Legacy Manager Falls Short
screens.narratorSegment: When projects grow, the legacy manager’s limitations become clear. The main issues are remapping difficulty, poor context management, and limited device coverage. Remapping is cumbersome because controls are tied to axis names in Project Settings; changing a binding often means editing central settings or adding custom runtime code. Contexts like gameplay, UI navigation, and cinematics require conditional checks in Update to enable or disable specific input uses. For multiple players or split-screen, the legacy approach forces complex naming conventions and custom routing. Device diversity is another challenge: modern gamepads, touch gestures, and XR controllers aren’t first-class citizens in the legacy setup, meaning extra work to translate their inputs into axes. A concrete example: supporting both WASD and gamepad left stick plus a touchscreen swipe typically needs separate code paths or brittle mapping. A common misconception is assuming code polling alone scales—polling still works, but it amplifies conditional complexity. The key takeaway is to recognize when your project’s input requirements have outgrown simple configured axes, and to choose a system that reduces branching and centralizes mappings. Where the Legacy Manager Falls Short means legacy input scales poorly when you need runtime remapping, context switching, multiple players, or broad device support.. In practical terms, remapping, contexts, and device diversity challenges. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Legacy Shortcomings
Comparison: Legacy limits
  • Remapping requires manual edits or custom runtime systems.
  • Context switching needs conditional polling logic in Update.
  • Supporting many device types needs bespoke bridging code.
Common mistake
Attempting to layer many conditional checks on top of Input.GetAxis instead of centralizing input logic.
Concrete scenario
You want WASD, arrow keys, left stick, and a touchscreen gesture to control movement. With the legacy manager, you must configure multiple axes or write per-device logic, increasing maintenance cost.
Key Takeaway

If you anticipate remapping, multiple device types, or different input contexts, the legacy manager will slow development and increase bugs.

screens.title: The Input System Package: Core Idea
screens.narratorSegment: The Input System Package reframes input as a set of named actions that describe player intent, not physical hardware. An action like Move or Jump is an abstract command. You then create bindings that connect physical controls—keyboard keys, gamepad buttons, sticks, or touch gestures—to those actions. Action Maps group related actions for a context, for example Gameplay or UI, and let you switch whole sets of input behavior cleanly. This abstraction enables runtime remapping and easier support for multiple devices and players because your game logic subscribes to actions, not to particular keys. A concrete example: define a Move action with control type Vector2 and bind WASD, arrow keys, and the left stick. The same action drives movement code regardless of where the input came from. A common misconception is that the new system is only about convenience; in fact it significantly improves maintainability and input fidelity. The takeaway is to think in actions and contexts rather than in raw device signals. The Input System Package: Core Idea means think in terms of actions and action maps; bind many devices to the same action for flexible, maintainable input handling.. In practical terms, actions, action maps, and device-agnostic input. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Input System Package
Core idea
Actions and Action Maps
Define abstract actions, then bind physical controls. Group actions into maps to manage contexts like Gameplay or UI.
Example
Move as Vector2 bound to WASD, arrows, and left stick. Jump as Button bound to Space and gamepad A.
Why it matters
Your gameplay code subscribes to actions, so input wiring changes without touching gameplay logic. This simplifies remapping and multi-device support.
Key Takeaway

Abstracting input as actions centralizes control mapping and reduces conditional branching in gameplay code.

screens.title: Install & Create an Input Action Asset
screens.narratorSegment: Installing the Input System Package and creating an Input Action Asset is the practical first step. Start in the Package Manager, select the Unity Registry, find the Input System, and click Install. Unity will usually prompt you to enable the new input backend and restart the editor; accept this to let the package take effect. After restart, right-click in the Project window and choose Create then Input Actions. Name the new asset PlayerControls. Open it to add an Action Map—call it Gameplay—and then add actions like Move and Jump. For Move, set the control type to Vector2; for Jump, set it to Button. Add bindings: for Move add a Gamepad left stick path and a 2D Vector composite mapped to WASD. For Jump add bindings for the Space key and the gamepad A button. Save the asset. A common oversight is forgetting to save the asset after editing, which loses your bindings. The final takeaway: follow this simple process to centralize input and make future remapping straightforward. In practical terms, step-by-step: package manager to playercontrols asset. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Install & Create Asset
Step-by-step
  1. Open Window → Package Manager and select Unity Registry, then install Input System.
  2. Accept editor restart when prompted to enable the new backend.
  3. In Project window: Create → Input Actions and name it PlayerControls.
  4. Open asset, add Action Map named Gameplay, add Move (Vector2) and Jump (Button).
  5. Add bindings: Gamepad left stick and 2D Vector composite for WASD; Space and gamepad A for Jump.
  6. Click Save Asset in the Input Actions editor.
Example bindings
Move: Path <Gamepad>/leftStick and 2D Vector composite WASD. Jump: Path <Keyboard>/space and <Gamepad>/aButton.
Key Takeaway

Follow the install and author workflow once; the Input Action Asset is your single source of truth for controls.

screens.title: Bindings and Control Types
screens.narratorSegment: Bindings link physical inputs to actions and specify the expected control type. The control type determines how the system interprets input data. For movement you typically use a Vector2 control type because it represents two-dimensional directional input from WASD, arrow keys, or a left joystick. For discrete actions like Jump you use a Button control type, which reports press and release events. The Input Actions editor also supports composites: for example a 2D Vector composite bundles Up, Down, Left, and Right into a single Vector2 binding, making WASD mapping straightforward. A concrete example: add a 2D Vector composite named WASD and assign the individual keys to Up, Down, Left, and Right, alongside a separate gamepad left stick binding; both produce a Vector2 value your movement code consumes. A common misconception is to treat everything as buttons or raw axis values; control types give semantic meaning that helps processors and interactions behave correctly. The takeaway: choose the control type that matches your action so bindings produce predictable values for gameplay code. Bindings and Control Types means use vector2 for directional movement, button for discrete inputs, and composites like 2d vector to map keyboard keys cleanly.. In practical terms, vector2 for movement, button for discrete actions, and composites. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Bindings & Control Types
Control types
Vector2 for directional movement, Button for discrete actions like Jump or Fire.
Composite example
Create a 2D Vector composite named WASD and map Up to W, Down to S, Left to A, Right to D.
Concrete example
Move action: Vector2 produced by either the WASD composite or <Gamepad>/leftStick binding. Jump action: Button produced by <Keyboard>/space and <Gamepad>/aButton.
Key Takeaway

Pick the control type that matches the semantic input. Composites simplify multi-key mappings into a single coherent value.

screens.title: Processors and Interactions
screens.narratorSegment: Processors and interactions are tools inside the Input Action Asset that shape how raw input is interpreted. Processors modify the value an action reports: for example a deadzone processor removes small stick drift, and a normalize processor turns a raw vector into a unit vector. Interactions describe how presses are interpreted: a Press interaction detects simple presses, a Hold interaction requires the input to be held for a duration, and Tap can differentiate quick taps from full presses. Concrete example: for a charged attack you might set Jump to use a Hold interaction so the action only fires after the player holds the button for a configured time. A common mistake is to ignore processors and then implement deadzone logic in gameplay code; that scatters input tuning across scripts. Proper use of processors and interactions centralizes feel adjustments in the Input Action Asset and keeps gameplay code focused on game rules. The main takeaway is to use processors and interactions to capture device quirks and player intent before your code receives the value. Processors and Interactions means use processors to clean or transform values and interactions to describe press behavior so gameplay code receives semantic input.. In practical terms, tuning values and defining input behaviors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Processors & Interactions
Processors
Modify values: deadzone, normalize, scale. Use them to correct device behavior before gameplay sees the input.
Interactions
Define how an input is interpreted: Press, Hold, Tap, and combinations to match gameplay needs.
Concrete scenario
For a charged jump, use a Hold interaction on Jump and a deadzone processor on left stick to avoid accidental triggers while idle.
Key Takeaway

Use processors and interactions to centralize input tuning and keep gameplay code clean and consistent.

screens.title: Event-driven Input: Subscribe to Actions
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most impactful differences in the new system is the move toward event-driven input. Instead of polling each frame with Input. GetAxis or Input. GetButton, you can subscribe to action events such as performed, started, and canceled. When a player presses Jump, your registered callback runs only when the action fires, which can reduce per-frame checks and clarify control flow. A concrete example: subscribe to Move. performed to receive a Vector2 value when the control changes and use that to set velocity in your movement controller. Many developers still poll actions in Update out of habit; this works but loses the clarity and efficiency of callbacks. A common misconception is that event-driven input is only for UI. In fact it's ideal for gameplay too, especially for discrete events like jump presses or attack triggers. The takeaway is to prefer subscriptions for event-driven behavior and use polling selectively when you need continuous sampling with precise timing. Event-driven Input: Subscribe to Actions means subscribe to action events like performed for cleaner, often more efficient input handling rather than constant polling.. In practical terms, avoid constant polling by using performed callbacks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The takeaway is to prefer subscriptions for event-driven behavior and use polling selectively when you need continuous sampling with precise timing. screens.title: Mixed Backends and Migration Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: A common migration pitfall is enabling the new Input System without fully updating scripts, leading to silent failures. Unity prompts to switch backends when installing the package; some developers accept and enable the new backend while leaving legacy code unchanged. In that case, Input. GetAxis calls may stop working because active input handling changed. You can set Active Input Handling to Both to temporarily support both systems, but this can introduce confusion and conflicts if both systems are reading the same devices differently. Another frequent mistake is trying to map old Input. GetAxis calls directly to new action bindings without embracing the action-based design; this leads to maintaining parallel code paths. A practical remedy is to migrate one action at a time: create the Input Action Asset, wire a new Move action, subscribe in code, and verify behavior before removing legacy polling. screens.title: How Action Maps Simplify Contexts
screens.narratorSegment: Action Maps let you group related actions and switch whole input contexts without scattered conditionals. For example, you can have a Gameplay action map with Move, Jump, and Attack, and a separate UI action map with Navigate, Submit, and Cancel. When a menu opens, you enable the UI map and disable Gameplay, ensuring that the same physical inputs perform UI navigation instead of moving the character. This eliminates the messy conditional checks in Update that often appear in legacy systems. A concrete example: on opening the inventory, disable Gameplay map and enable UI map; the Move action in Gameplay no longer receives input and the Navigate action in UI responds to arrow keys or a gamepad stick. The key takeaway is to map actions by context and toggle maps as your game state changes for predictable and maintainable behavior. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll build a practical understanding of how Unity handles player input, and why the modern Input System Package is a different way of thinking. Historically, Unity exposed input through the Input class and a set of named axes and buttons. That worked for simple cases but became hard to scale as control schemes grew. The new Input System flips the approach: you define actions like Jump or Move, then map multiple physical controls to those actions. You’ll learn when to keep the legacy manager, when to adopt the package, and how to set up an Input Action Asset that makes runtime remapping and multiple control schemes manageable. We’ll also cover action maps, bindings, processors and interactions so you can make inputs feel responsive. By the end you will be able to configure a PlayerControls asset that supports keyboard and gamepad movement, and you’ll know the common migration mistakes to avoid. Think about your last game prototype: could abstracting inputs into actions simplify your code and make controls more robust for players?

These objectives focus your work with Unity’s input systems so you learn both theory and practice. First, you will be able to differentiate between the legacy Input Manager and the Input System Package: know the role of Input. GetAxis and configured axes versus action-based mappings. Second, you will understand why the Input System Package is advantageous for flexibility, remapping, and multi-device support by exploring action maps, bindings, and event-driven callbacks. Third, you will configure the Input System Package in a project and create an Input Action Asset that defines action maps like Gameplay and UI plus actions like Move and Jump. Fourth, you will identify common pitfalls when migrating—such as disabling legacy input unexpectedly or misusing processors—and plan remedies. Each objective pairs a concrete task with a reason why it matters so you can both perform the steps and evaluate when to adopt the new system in real projects.

This second objectives slide ties each goal to a measurable practice so you can prove competency. For differentiation, inspect a project that uses Input. GetAxis and identify at least two limitations in mapping and multiple device support. For understanding advantages, set up a small scene with both keyboard and gamepad bindings to the same action and observe remapping behavior. For configuration skills, actually install the Input System Package and create a PlayerControls Input Action Asset with a Gameplay action map containing Move and Jump. For migration awareness, intentionally enable both input systems in a test project and observe which calls stop working, then revert to a single system or migrate scripts to subscribe to action events. Each practice step turns conceptual knowledge into hands-on evidence you can include in a developer log or checklist.

The legacy Input Manager is Unity’s original way of getting player input. It centers on the Input class and a set of named axes and buttons configured in Project Settings. In practice you call functions like Input. GetAxis with a logical axis name such as Horizontal, and Unity returns a float based on keyboard or joystick input mapped to that axis. This approach made small projects easy because you could centralize mappings and poll in Update. A concrete example is movement: many projects use an axis named Horizontal that maps the A and D keys, left and right arrow keys, and the joystick X-axis. That single axis return value drives character motion. A common misconception is that this system automatically supports many devices: it does work for keyboards and basic gamepads but struggles with diverse devices, fine-grained remapping, or separate control contexts. The main takeaway is that the legacy manager works well when control requirements are simple and fixed, but it becomes brittle as you add remapping, multiple players, or XR controllers. Keep this definition in mind when we compare it to the action-based model that follows.

When projects grow, the legacy manager’s limitations become clear. The main issues are remapping difficulty, poor context management, and limited device coverage. Remapping is cumbersome because controls are tied to axis names in Project Settings; changing a binding often means editing central settings or adding custom runtime code. Contexts like gameplay, UI navigation, and cinematics require conditional checks in Update to enable or disable specific input uses. For multiple players or split-screen, the legacy approach forces complex naming conventions and custom routing. Device diversity is another challenge: modern gamepads, touch gestures, and XR controllers aren’t first-class citizens in the legacy setup, meaning extra work to translate their inputs into axes. A concrete example: supporting both WASD and gamepad left stick plus a touchscreen swipe typically needs separate code paths or brittle mapping. A common misconception is assuming code polling alone scales—polling still works, but it amplifies conditional complexity. The key takeaway is to recognize when your project’s input requirements have outgrown simple configured axes, and to choose a system that reduces branching and centralizes mappings. Where the Legacy Manager Falls Short means legacy input scales poorly when you need runtime remapping, context switching, multiple players, or broad device support.. In practical terms, remapping, contexts, and device diversity challenges. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Input System Package reframes input as a set of named actions that describe player intent, not physical hardware. An action like Move or Jump is an abstract command. You then create bindings that connect physical controls—keyboard keys, gamepad buttons, sticks, or touch gestures—to those actions. Action Maps group related actions for a context, for example Gameplay or UI, and let you switch whole sets of input behavior cleanly. This abstraction enables runtime remapping and easier support for multiple devices and players because your game logic subscribes to actions, not to particular keys. A concrete example: define a Move action with control type Vector2 and bind WASD, arrow keys, and the left stick. The same action drives movement code regardless of where the input came from. A common misconception is that the new system is only about convenience; in fact it significantly improves maintainability and input fidelity. The takeaway is to think in actions and contexts rather than in raw device signals. In practical terms, actions, action maps, and device-agnostic input. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Installing the Input System Package and creating an Input Action Asset is the practical first step. Start in the Package Manager, select the Unity Registry, find the Input System, and click Install. Open it to add an Action Map—call it Gameplay—and then add actions like Move and Jump. For Move, set the control type to Vector2; for Jump, set it to Button. For movement you typically use a Vector2 control type because it represents two-dimensional directional input from WASD, arrow keys, or a left joystick. For discrete actions like Jump you use a Button control type, which reports press and release events. Let's restate the essential terms you'll use regularly. First, the Input Manager refers to Unity's legacy system where inputs are configured as named axes and polled via the Input class. Third, the Input Action Asset is the central configuration asset that contains action maps, actions, bindings, processors, and interactions. Finish by reinforcing the operational pieces you’ll use daily. An Action is the abstract command like Move or Jump. A Binding links a specific physical control to an action, such as Space or the gamepad A button. Processors transform raw input values—deadzone and normalize are common examples—so your gameplay code receives predictable data. Interactions define how input is interpreted over time, such as Press or Hold. Keep these distinctions in mind: actions define intent, bindings connect devices, processors tune values, and interactions capture timing and intent nuances.
